347.title: Changes in solid materials when bent, pressed, hammered, and cut

members.title: Changes in solid materials when bent, pressed, hammered, and cut
members.content: The image shows four distinct ways a solid material can be altered. The first shows a shape change where a long piece is bent into a curve, but the overall size remains the same. Next, a flat piece is shown being pressed, resulting in a flattened shape and the original amount of material remaining unchanged. The third depicts a piece of metal being hammered, which causes it to become flattened and widened, and importantly, the metal itself remains solid. Finally, the image displays a piece being cut, resulting in two smaller pieces, each retaining the same material as the original.

347.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 1 of 3)

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
The Grade 5 competency moves from force to two conditions that cause deeper changes: application of heat and the presence or lack of oxygen.
Heat can cause a material to melt, evaporate, soften, harden, or burn.
Ice left on a saucer melts into water.

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Candle wax melts and then hardens again when it cools.
Sugar heated in a pan turns brown and gives off a sweet smell as it becomes caramel — and that change cannot be undone.
Oxygen is part of the air around us, and many changes depend on whether it is present.

members.title: Changes Caused by Heat and by Oxygen (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Iron exposed to air and moisture forms a reddish-brown coating called rust, which is why a bakal na pako left outdoors during the rainy season looks nothing like a new one.
A candle covered by a glass jar goes out because the oxygen inside is used up.
Sliced saging or mansanas turns brown when left on the table because its exposed flesh reacts with the oxygen in the air.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
By Grade 6, learners sort changes into two kinds.
A physical change alters only the appearance of a material — its size, shape, or state — while the material itself stays the same.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Physical changes are usually reversible: melted ice can be frozen again, a crumpled paper can be flattened, and dissolved salt can be recovered by evaporating the water.
A chemical change produces an entirely new material with new properties.

members.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Chemical changes are irreversible: rust cannot be turned back into shiny iron, burnt wood cannot be turned back into wood, and a cooked egg cannot be uncooked.
Useful clues that a chemical change has taken place are a new color, a new smell, bubbles of gas, heat given off, or a solid forming where there was none.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 1 of 3)
members.content:
The last Grade 4 competency asks learners to judge a change, not just describe it.
Many changes are useful.
Cutting cloth produces clothing.
Hammering metal produces tools.
Cooking makes food safe and easier to digest.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 2 of 3)
members.content:
Decaying leaves in a compost pit become fertilizer for a school garden.
Other changes are harmful, especially to the environment.
Rust weakens roofing sheets and bridges.
Spoiled food causes illness.

members.title: Useful and Harmful Changes (Part 3 of 3)
members.content:
Burning plastic and other household waste releases smoke and toxic gases into the air, which is why the practice is discouraged and is covered by the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act.
Learning to tell useful changes from harmful ones is what turns this lesson from a list of observations into a habit of responsible decision-making.

357.title: The main parts of a flower involved in reproduction

members.title: The main parts of a flower involved in reproduction
members.content: The image shows the key components of a flower involved in reproduction. At the top, the stamen is positioned first, consisting of a filament supporting an anther, which produces pollen. Below the stamen is the pistil, comprising the ovary and style, with the style leading to an ovule within the ovary, where egg cells are stored. The petals and sepals surround these central parts of the flower, providing protection and attracting pollinators.

members.title: The main parts of a flower involved in reproduction
members.content: The image shows a flower with several distinct parts arranged around a central core. At the top, there are multiple, slender stalks, called filaments, supporting a cluster of small, rounded structures – these are the anthers, which produce pollen. Below the anthers, and extending downwards, is a central, elongated structure – the pistil – which is composed of a sticky, top part called the stigma, and a shorter, tube-like section known as the style. At the base of the pistil is a swollen, rounded structure called the ovary, which contains the egg cells.

members.title: Reproduction in Flowering Plants
members.content: Flowering plants reproduce sexually, which means a new plant begins when a male sex cell joins a female sex cell. Most of this activity happens inside the flower, which is the reproductive part of the plant. A single flower can contain both male and female parts, and these parts work together so that seeds can form. Seeds later grow into new plants, allowing the species to continue.

members.title: Reproduction in Flowering Plants (Part 1 of 2)
members.content:
Flowering plants reproduce sexually, which means a new plant begins when a male sex cell joins a female sex cell.
Most of this activity happens inside the flower, which is the reproductive part of the plant.

members.title: Reproduction in Flowering Plants (Part 2 of 2)
members.content:
A single flower can contain both male and female parts, and these parts work together so that seeds can form.
Seeds later grow into new plants, allowing the species to continue.
Male parts (the stamen) produce pollen; female parts (the pistil) hold the egg cells.

members.title: Stamen (Male Part)
members.content: The stamen is made up of the anther and the filament. The filament is the thin stalk that holds up the anther, while the anther produces tiny grains called pollen. Each pollen grain carries a male sex cell.

members.title: Stamen (Male Part)
members.content: The stamen is made up of the anther and the filament. The filament is the thin stalk that holds up the anther, while the anther produces tiny grains called pollen. Each pollen grain carries a male sex cell.

members.title: Pistil (Female Part)
members.content: The pistil, also called the carpel, is made up of the stigma, style, and ovary. The sticky stigma catches pollen, the style connects the stigma to the ovary, and the ovary contains ovules. Each ovule holds a female sex cell, or egg.

members.title: Pistil (Female Part)
members.content: The pistil, also called the carpel, is made up of the stigma, style, and ovary. The sticky stigma catches pollen, the style connects the stigma to the ovary, and the ovary contains ovules. Each ovule holds a female sex cell, or egg.

members.title: Petals and Sepals (Supporting Parts)
members.content:
The colorful petals attract pollinators such as bees, butterflies, and birds. The green sepals protect the flower while it is still a bud.
These parts do not make sex cells, but they help reproduction succeed.

members.title: Petals and Sepals (Supporting Parts)
members.content: The colorful petals attract pollinators such as bees, butterflies, and birds. The green sepals protect the flower while it is still a bud. These parts do not make sex cells, but they help reproduction succeed.

members.title: Pollination
members.content: Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma. This can happen within the same flower or between different flowers, with the help of wind, water, insects, or other animals.

members.title: Pollination
members.content: Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma. This can happen within the same flower or between different flowers, with the help of wind, water, insects, or other animals.

members.title: Fertilization
members.content: After landing on the stigma, a pollen grain grows a tube down the style into the ovary. The male sex cell then joins the egg cell inside an ovule.

members.title: Fertilization
members.content: After landing on the stigma, a pollen grain grows a tube down the style into the ovary. The male sex cell then joins the egg cell inside an ovule.

members.title: Seed formation
members.content: The fertilized ovule develops into a seed, which contains a tiny young plant and a store of food.

members.title: Seed formation
members.content: The fertilized ovule develops into a seed, which contains a tiny young plant and a store of food.

members.title: Fruit formation
members.content: The ovary grows into a fruit that surrounds and protects the seeds and helps them spread to new places.

members.title: Fruit formation
members.content: The ovary grows into a fruit that surrounds and protects the seeds and helps them spread to new places.

members.title: Everyday Examples
members.content: A gumamela (hibiscus) shows all the flower parts clearly, which is why it is often used in class. A mango tree flowers, is pollinated, and then forms the mango fruit with a seed inside. Rice plants are pollinated mostly by wind, while many fruit trees depend on bees. These examples show that pollination and fertilization must happen first before a seed or fruit can form, and each seed carries the beginnings of a brand-new plant.
